title: U.S. envoy says a strike on Iran could come 'this weekend' — Trump says he knows nothing about it
excerpt: U.S. envoy Tom Barrack said Friday a strike on Iran could come as soon as this weekend, while President Trump publicly played down the prospect and oil prices jumped past $117 a barrel.
content:
The United States could strike Iran as soon as this weekend, U.S. envoy Tom Barrack said Friday — while President Donald Trump, asked about the remarks the same day, said he knew nothing about any such plan.

"Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely," Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria, said in an interview on the Mario Nawfal podcast while visiting the Gulf, according to Agence France-Presse. Barrack added that Trump remains "open and available and accessible to a deal" after months of stalled negotiations.

Barrack also drew a line the White House has repeated: any U.S. action would not aim to overthrow Iran's government. "The consequence won't be regime change," he said. "The problem with regime change always is, what's the day-two scenario?"

That position contrasts with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections Tuesday and has repeatedly vowed in recent days to topple Iran's clerical state, following two major bombing campaigns against it since last year.

Asked in Florida about Barrack's comments, Trump played down the possibility of an imminent strike, saying: "If that's the case, I don't know anything about it." Trump has previously signaled he could resume military action against Iran, but had indicated major action would not come before the U.S. congressional elections on November 3.

Tensions have risen all week. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they struck four commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, Houthi rebels in Yemen have stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, and the U.S. State Department ordered the departure of non-essential personnel from its embassy in Saudi Arabia. Iran has warned it would hit Gulf oil facilities, undersea cables, data centers and AI facilities if a new U.S.-Israeli offensive is launched.

Markets reacted immediately: Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, rose about 3.5 percent on Friday to pass $117 a barrel at one point — its highest level since April — before easing to just over $116. It traded around $72 in February, before the war, and peaked near $126 at the end of April.

What it means for readers here

No strike has been confirmed, and the public record right now is a split screen: an envoy warning of war and a president claiming ignorance. What is confirmed is the oil-price jump, and sustained crude prices at this level have historically worked their way to the pump in South Texas over days and weeks. Webb Watch 956 will keep watching gas prices in Laredo alongside the diplomacy — and will update this story if the White House, Tehran or any official source confirms or rules out military action.
